newsitem.title: USA: Looking back on people of 1996.
newsitem.headline: Looking back on people of 1996.

text.p: - Time to ring in the New Year, but not before a parting glance at a few of the famous and not-so-famous people previously highlighted in this space who made the Internet what it was during the past 12 months.

It's been almost a year since Cathy Murtha started her campaign to make Web sites accessible to the blind and vision-impaired. Since then, Murtha, a blind 37-year-old mother of three from Pioneer, Calif., has become an unofficial spokeswoman for blind Internet users. She writes a "Webability" column for the Web Designers Gazette, has spoken at a National Federation of the Blind state convention and established a "Speech-Friendly Ribbon Award" given to Web sites that make accommodations for people who use screen-reader software to surf the net.
"People are listening," she said.

Murtha and partner Tom Baccanti also started a company, Magical Mist Creations, that designs accessible Web sites and sells tutorials on accessibility. (Find out more at Murtha's Web site, http://www2.cdepot.net/mist).
On top of it all, Murtha has maintained a 4.0 grade point average at her local community college, where she is studying with the goal of becoming a teacher or writer.
"It's been an incredible year," she said.

Chris Hassett could say the same thing. Last January, Hassett was putting the finishing touches on a new service that brings channels of headline news and advertising to an idle computer screen. The PointCast (http://www.pointcast.com/) service launched in February and by summer was one of the biggest buzzes of the industry, the advance guard of the new "push" Internet business model where software or other technology brings information to a person's computer rather than making them seek it out on the Web.

By early December, PointCast had 1.7 million viewers generating more than 50 million hits a day, partnerships with major newspapers throughout the country, a stable of 140 advertisers, $48 million in investments and a deal with Microsoft that will embed PointCast in the next version of Windows 95, due in the second half of 1997.
It's no wonder the Web-based publication cnet (http://www.cnet.com/) recently named the former electrical engineer its "Newsmaker of the Year."

"It comes down to finding an area you can pioneer and delivering on that something that's fundamentally useful to people," Hassett said. "I know we've found that because I go into people's offices who never used the Net and they're using PointCast."
The New Year is looking a little brighter for Michael Hart, but only a little.

Hart is founder and proprietor of Project Gutenberg (http://www.etext.org/Gutenberg/pg/pg_home.html), a 21-year-old volunteer effort to transcribe classic works of literature and historical documents into electronic texts free to anyone on the Internet.

Earlier this year, Hart lost must of his financial support when two universities declined to continue funding, and royalties slipped after sales of CD-ROM versions of Gutenberg texts dropped dramatically. In early December, Hart and his volunteer crew of 700 were still working, but their prospects for continuing much past Jan. 1 looked bleak.
But in an interview Tuesday, Hart said he had some leads on financing.
"It's not quite as dark at the end of the tunnel, there may be some fireflies," he said.
Despite his dire financial straits, Hart's not thinking of charging for access to Gutenberg texts, which number close to 700.
"Half the offers we get are from people who want to take us over," he said. "I don't want them to own it and sell the stuff rather than give it away."

All systems are go for Alex Hempton and Youth Central (http://www.youthcentral.apple.com/), the online teen community he helped create for Apple Computer. Hempton was all of 13 when he started Youth Central two years ago on Apple's eWorld service and has served as Webmaster ever since, including supervising its relocation to the Web after Apple shelved the online network last March.
These days, Hempton is preparing to add live chat to the site and investigating whether to begin accepting advertising. A major redesign is slated for March.
"We're experimenting with Java and animation, sound and Quicktime (movie software) and virtual reality. Since it's sponsored by Apple, we have access to a lot of technology Apple has," Hempton said.
Hempton, a sophomore at Scripps Ranch High School in San Diego, was invited to talk about Youth Central before the International Institute of Communications in Munich, Germany, this fall.
"What we want to do eventually is localise Youth Central so people in Germany or with other languages can connect in their own language," he said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter@deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
